summary: # Marvelous Designer 2024.0: Nave Espacial Tutorial ## Introduction Welcome to a new Marvelous Designer tutorial. In this tutorial, we will cover the creation of the spacecraft that you can see in the February informative bulletin. We will see how to plan the creation of a project to combine Hull Surface with modeling in Marvelous Designer. ## Conceptualizing the Spacecraft First, you must be clear about the concept of the spacecraft and its objectives. To have a conceptual base, we create a stable foundation on which to work. Here, we can see the final result, with the base patterns and avatars used. The base patterns of the body of the spacecraft are frozen or deactivated, and we only use an avatar for the creation of the spacecraft. Both the base of the body and the propeller are created in external software. Even so, they are two different processes when it comes to using these resources. ## Importing Patterns We have two options for the base: import as OBJ, Garment, or CBX Avatar. Since we want a representation of the patterns in the 2D window, we import as OBJ and activate the 2D window. The box "Trace Maps UV" will create the UVs from the 2D patterns, allowing us to work directly on these patterns. The imported object will maintain the shape with which it was created, helping to maintain the curves of the body of the spacecraft and acting as a 2D pattern. ## Dividing the Spacecraft Body Let's start by drawing the different sections in which we want to divide the body of the spacecraft. This is where we can test different possibilities and designs, giving ourselves the freedom to experiment. After selecting the different options, the results will be like this: in my case, this was my design. ## Creating Layers We create a layer, this time on top of our base. We want it to keep the seams with its original pattern. The fewer seams you have to do manually in a project with so many internal lines, the better, as this avoids possible failures. Thus, doing a cloning top or bottom will help us in the process. We unbind the linked edition, select a sectioned area, and cut it. With the different areas, it will be easier to work by being able to deactivate those that we are not editing. ## Managing Cuts and Seams Remember that for each line you cut, you will have to create a seam to the base pattern in the same cut lines. Finally, we will have the basic patterns, which will be those that we have not cut, and the cut patterns, which will be our 3D object. After creating the basic patterns, we will add its three elements to the base pattern that we have already cut in the previous project. We must make a pattern that takes into account the important points we already know and hide them. We will use clay, for example. ## Pattern Visibility and Adjustments At this step, we can deactivate the pattern—only the pattern, not the seams—so while we simulate the 3D object, it will maintain the curvature. We will change the patterns in the 2D window for better visualization. We edit each part according to the design. In our case, we will give a larger size to the superimposed patterns so that they have greater extension, adding more folds and details. ## Scaling Patterns We will also change the size of the 3D object. All my IIIc2 patterns will be scaled; if not, their shape would be too close to the base patterns without proper expression. ## Working with Front and Side Panels In this pattern chosen for the example, it is visible how a small variation in the scale affects its visibility. Let's see some other sectioned areas of the ship. We apply certain properties to the front panel that will give it a more rigid appearance despite increasing its size. It is distributed in a grid, with each line having two lines displaced to one side and the other. These lines will have bending force properties of 30 and a bending angle of 225, creating slightly protruding areas compared to the rest. ## Additional Properties for Side Panel For the side panel, I want to give an effect with a large number of folds but with suction—an effect that is given with recurrence to fabrics that cover structures exposed to space. We click on the properties panel and press 20. ## Elastic Properties All lines have the elastic properties activated with a strength value of 10 and a ratio of 80, to increase the freezing plain expressions. Try using an irregular pattern model. As you can see, the size of the pattern is again larger than the base pattern; if the size is not large enough, you cannot see any kind of expression in your patterns compared to the base pattern. ## Mirroring and Connections With pieces that you have planned to make a mirror, you will have to choose whether you are going to sew the connected parts or if they are going to go separately. This particular piece does not need to be sewn in the connections of both patterns, so we can make a reflected copy. As it is a finished part, it will remain frozen and will not require a base to maintain its position or simulate again. ## Internal Lines and Repetition In this section, I will simply apply internal lines and repeat throughout the pattern, applying elastic to these internal lines with a force of 10 and a ratio of 32. In the design of the ship, this area will be covered by the hard surface, so it does not need to be joined. ## Symmetry and Seams We will perform the reverse case, ensuring that the connected parts are joined. If we do a copy-paste reflected, like the previous piece, the result will not be natural. We will carry out symmetry with seams, both to the base piece and to the superimposed pattern. If we have established the symmetry values, then the key will be distinguishable. This is useful for any pattern, but it is not useful when we play with the design. ## Naturalizing the Silhouette We place the tool "JOIN" in the alignment lines to naturalize the silhouette to the singular form. Here at the top of the pattern, we place the hook slightly elevated compared to others. By including the base pattern in the reflected copy, it will allow us to simulate without worrying about the seams. ## Performance Optimization If we carry out projects with a high polygonal load, in which many parts do not collide with each other, we use freeze or deactivate to isolate the parts that you want to simulate and improve performance. ## Final Simulation Techniques By using the same technique as in the square pattern, you can obtain a series of patterns with a more rigid appearance. This will help you create pieces that cover areas not strongly expressive in folds and that are close to a hard surface modeling style. ## Conclusion and Exporting After the creation of the body, we will make an example of how you can use parts of the ship as an avatar and others as GACMEN, facilitating our creation process while respecting the limits of our design. To create the propeller, I import the propulsor as a GACMEN. I import as FBX Avatar so that it interacts with the patterns that cover it. I also import a selected loop of the propeller as OBJ Garment to serve as an anchor, along with the back of the ship to facilitate the sewing of the pattern. This is the aspect after simulating our pattern. In the 2D viewer, we can see it clearly identified as the white pattern. The shorter width is sewn to the selected loop of the propeller, while the longer width connects to the back of the ship. These two frozen patterns will not be visible during the render, so once you are happy with the result, you can remove them before exporting. Finally, we export as FBX and join the design parts created in Marvelous Designer to the rest of the ship in the rendering software that you prefer. In my case, this would be the result of our project. We hope that these techniques will help you create similar projects by combining Marvelous Designer and Hard Surface.
